1.pericope_label: After these things Paul departed from Athens, and came to Corinth; and found a certain Jew named Aquila, lately come from Italy with his wife Priscilla

schools.summary: Corinth is described as the antithesis of Athens: Barnes calls it "the Paris of antiquity" where lasciviousness was consecrated in the worship of Venus, and Robertson counts a thousand temple prostitutes on the Acrocorinthus and a verb meaning to live immorally. Both trace the city's destruction by Mummius and refoundation by Julius Caesar; Robertson reads Aquila's bare description as a Jew, not yet a disciple, and dates Claudius's edict about A.D. 49, agreeing that Suetonius's Chrestus stands for Christ.

Calvin takes the improbability of the mission as the argument: Paul enters a rich and crowded city "a simple man, unknown, having no eloquence or pomp", and the result proves the Spirit rather than the means. He then reads Aquila's double exile as providence rather than misfortune, since "the Lord doth often better provide for us when he doth sharply punish us", and Gill labours to distinguish this Aquila from the Greek translator and from Onkelos.

Clarke supplies the historical apparatus — the Corinthian order of architecture, the reduced modern city — and then breaks with the consensus on Suetonius, refusing to identify Chrestus with Christ ("how could he intend Christ, who was never at Rome?") and insisting he was a real agitator. He also denies that Aquila and Priscilla were yet Christians, making their conversion the fruit of Paul's lodging with them. Wesley explains the failure at Athens by the philosophers' self-satisfaction.

Henry notes that Paul left Athens unpersecuted — the reception was merely cold — and passes on the proverb that not every man may see Corinth, together with the observation that Aquila often changed his habitation, "this is not the world we can propose ourselves a settlement in".

debates.question: Is Suetonius's "Chrestus" a mistake for Christ?

positions.view: Yes — a Roman historian, little acquainted with Jewish affairs, mistook disputes about Christ for a living ringleader; Barnes builds five steps to the conclusion and Robertson dates the edict about A.D. 49.
No — Christ was never at Rome and no one personated him there; Chrestus "is no fictitious name, no name of an absent person, nor of a sect", but a real agitator who probably suffered for it.

debates.question: Were Aquila and Priscilla already Christians when Paul found them?

positions.view: It is evident that Aquila had become a convert to the Christian faith.
There is no evidence of it; their conversion was most likely the fruit of Paul's lodging with them.
Luke's bare "a Jew from Pontus" implies he was apparently not yet a disciple.

debates.question: Is this Aquila the translator, or Onkelos?

positions.view: Neither — the proselyte Aquila who made the Greek version and Onkelos the Chaldee paraphrast differ from him in name, nation and date.
He may well be the Onkelos of the Jewish writers.
Notes only that the translator was also from Pontus, and leaves the coincidence alone.

outliers.view: Reads Paul's only lodging in Corinth being a twice-exiled man as instruction rather than hardship: "this happy calamity of Aquila doth teach us, that the Lord doth often better provide for us when he doth sharply punish us."

themes: After these things Paul departed from Athens, and came to Corinth;
And found a certain Jew named Aquila, born in Pontus, lately come from Italy, with his wife Priscilla; (because that Claudius had commanded all Jews to depart from Rome:) and came unto them.

3.pericope_label: And because he was of the same craft, he abode with them, and wrought; and he reasoned in the synagogue every sabbath

schools.summary: Barnes and Robertson treat the trade as ordinary Jewish practice — Robertson quoting Rabbi Judah that not teaching a son a trade is teaching him to steal — while disputing what the trade was: a weaver of tapestry (as Luther translated), or a maker of tents from leather or goat's hair. On v.5 all three grammarians take the better reading to be "constrained by the word" rather than "pressed in spirit", though Robertson breaks with the translators by making the verb a direct middle, and Ellicott and Robertson then divide over what intensified Paul's preaching.

Calvin explains the manual labour strategically rather than from need: the false apostles taught without charge in order to "craftily creep in", and Paul would not concede them the advantage. He dismisses the Latin addition "interposing the name of the Lord Jesus" as a copyist's patch, and describes a deliberately indirect method — corrupt nature, the necessity of grace, the promised Redeemer as "a fit and brief preparation unto Christ" — with the rule that teachers should consider where to begin. Gill draws out the weekly rhythm of sabbath preaching and weekday work.

Clarke canvasses every proposed meaning of the trade and gives up honestly — "in short, we know not what the trade was" — then turns the verse into a defence of working preachers against the clergy who despise them. He argues at length that the manuscripts require "constrained by the word", and closes by noting that Silas vanishes from the record here, "probably he died in Macedonia". Wesley turns the Jewish custom of teaching every child a trade into a question for Christians.

debates.question: Was Paul "pressed in spirit" or "constrained by the word"?

positions.view: The better manuscripts read "the word"; Griesbach took it into the text and Clarke says there can be no doubt of it, Ellicott describing the Word within him as a constraining power.
Accepts the reading but disputes the voice: the verb is a direct middle, so Paul held himself wholly to preaching instead of only on sabbaths.
Keep the received text and read an inward impulse, Wesley urging every Christian to watch for such pressure and follow it where it agrees with Scripture.

debates.question: Why did Paul's preaching intensify when Silas and Timothy arrived?

positions.view: The gifts they brought from Macedonia released him from the tentmaking bench for a season.
Refuses that explanation — "there is no indication of his giving up tent-making" — and suggests instead that contact with people lately from Rome revived a long-cherished desire to preach there.
Simply the news the two men brought from Thessalonica.

debates.question: Why did Paul work with his hands at Corinth?

positions.view: Plain necessity — "it seems pretty evident that it was because he had no other means of maintenance".
Strategy — the false apostles taught freely so as to creep in craftily, and Paul refused to give them that advantage.

outliers.view: Turns the tentmaking into a defence of the working preacher against his critics: "how many of the clergy, and other ministers, are farmers, graziers, schoolmasters, and sleeping partners in different trades and commercial concerns! A tent-maker, in his place, is as useful as any of these."

themes: And because he was of the same craft, he abode with them, and wrought: for by their occupation they were tentmakers.
And he reasoned in the synagogue every sabbath, and persuaded the Jews and the Greeks.
And when Silas and Timotheus were come from Macedonia, Paul was pressed in the spirit, and testified to the Jews that Jesus was Christ.

6.pericope_label: And when they opposed themselves, and blasphemed, he shook his raiment, and said unto them, Your blood be upon your own heads

schools.summary: The grammarians read the opposition as organised — a verb of ranging in battle array — and the shaken raiment as a prophetic sign rather than temper, Robertson borrowing Ramsay's "undoubtedly a very exasperating gesture" and insisting the blood-formula is "a solemn disclaimer of responsibility", not a curse. Ellicott, alert that a Jew is doing this to Jews, calls it the last resource of one met by clamour instead of argument, and both he and Barnes limit the turn to the Gentiles to Corinth. On Justus they divide: Ellicott weighs the identification with the Titus of the epistles and refuses to decide, Robertson decides briskly against it.

Calvin watches the escalation from gainsaying to blaspheming as the ordinary progress of licence, makes the shaken garment "zeal kindled by God" rather than private indignation, and turns Ezekiel's charge on the ministry: teachers must "do what in them lieth to bring those which go astray into the way". Alone among the voices he reads the turn to the Gentiles nationally, as an inheritance transferred to shame Israel; and he suggests Paul chose the house next the synagogue "that he might the more nettle the Jews", inferring from Sosthenes's later title that Crispus was one chief man among several.

Clarke supplies the Nehemiah parallel for the shaken lap and dates the shaking-out of the nation sixteen years later, but also extends the verse into a standing charge against the Jews of his own century. He alone has Paul actually change lodgings to Justus's house, and lists what the synagogue ruler's office carried — presiding, interpreting, excommunicating, marrying, divorcing — supposing Sosthenes filled the vacant seat. Wesley limits the turn to the Gentiles narrowly: "only he preached no more in their synagogue".

Henry denies that Paul moved house at all — the change was of meeting-place, not lodging — and prefers charity to provocation as the reason for the adjoining door: Paul "would come as near to them as he could", ready to return if received.

debates.question: How far does "from henceforth I will go unto the Gentiles" reach?

positions.view: Local and limited — Paul gave up the Corinthian synagogue, not the nation, and preached to Jews afterwards at Ephesus and Rome.
National — the inheritance is taken from Israel and given to the Gentiles, partly to provoke them to repentance, though being incurable they got only despair from it.

debates.question: Did Paul move his lodging to the house of Justus?

positions.view: Yes — he departed from his former lodging and went "to lodge with Justus".
No — he continued with Aquila and Priscilla and went to the house only to preach, Calvin adding that the move was to come nearer the Gentiles rather than from weariness of his hosts.

debates.question: Why was the meeting-house next door to the synagogue?

positions.view: Charity — Paul came as near to them as he could, ready to return if they would receive his message.
Provocation — he chose that house "that he might the more nettle the Jews".
Unknowable — "whether Paul chose this location for his work because it was next to the synagogue, we do not know, but it caught the attendants at the synagogue worship".

outliers.view: Draws from the conversion of a synagogue ruler in so corrupt a city the wider inference that if a church could be organised at Corinth it can be organised anywhere, and "there is none so corrupt that the gospel cannot change and purify it".

themes: And when they opposed themselves, and blasphemed, he shook his raiment, and said unto them, Your blood be upon your own heads; I am clean: from henceforth I will go unto the Gentiles.
And he departed thence, and entered into a certain man’s house, named Justus, one that worshipped God, whose house joined hard to the synagogue.
And Crispus, the chief ruler of the synagogue, believed on the Lord with all his house; and many of the Corinthians hearing believed, and were baptized.

9.pericope_label: Then spake the Lord to Paul in the night by a vision, Be not afraid, but speak, and hold not thy peace

schools.summary: The grammarians locate the fear precisely: Barnes in the learning and splendour of the city and Paul's own "weakness, and fear, and much trembling", Ellicott in the social gap between his slave-class converts and men of his own culture, Robertson in a letter written at the same moment. Robertson presses the tenses — "stop being afraid, but go on speaking" — and reads the promise of much people as conditional on Paul holding on; Ellicott declines the dogmatics and hears Elijah's seven thousand. Barnes and Gill differ over how long Paul stayed at Ephesus.

Calvin refuses the word "dream", since Scripture distinguishes visions from dreams, and makes the oracle a remedy given only when necessity required it. He draws a rule from the pairing of the commands — fear does not merely silence a man but makes him speak guardedly, so "speak not with half thy mouth" — and qualifies the protection carefully: Paul was not spared violence, only frustrated attempts. On "much people" he grounds the title in the book of life, since "many sheep wander without the flock for a time". Gill reports the appearance as a dream.

Clarke reads a concrete plot behind the promise — "no man shall be permitted to lay violent hands upon thee" — and shifts the ground of "much people" away from decree to response: they are those "who have not resisted my Spirit, and consequently are now under its teachings", ready when the gospel reaches them. He thinks both Thessalonian letters, and perhaps Galatians, were written in this interval. Wesley is briefest of all, calling them prophetically "them that afterward believed".

debates.question: What does "I have much people in this city" mean?

positions.view: A fixed decree — "there is no chance; no hap-hazard" — those spoken of being God's already, before conversion, and written in the book of life.
Not decree but non-resistance: they are people who have not resisted the Spirit and are already under its teaching, ready when the gospel reaches them.
A prophetic way of speaking — he calls them his who would afterward believe.
Election with a condition attached to the outcome: they are "not yet saved, but who will be if Paul holds on".
Declines the dogmatic question and hears the echo of Elijah's seven thousand — souls in whom conscience was not yet dead.

debates.question: Was the appearance a dream or a vision?

positions.view: Christ appeared to him asleep, in a dream.
Not a dream — Scripture distinguishes the two, and Paul was in a trance and "saw a certain shape or form whereby he knew that God was present with him".

debates.question: How long was Paul at Ephesus?

positions.view: Two years — the only place where he stayed longer than the eighteen months at Corinth.
Three years.

outliers.view: Turns the contrast between the two cities into a rule about where the gospel prospers: "Paul had little success in philosophic Athens; he had great success in dissolute Corinth" — there is often more hope of an openly dissolute man than of one confident in his own wisdom.

themes: Then spake the Lord to Paul in the night by a vision, Be not afraid, but speak, and hold not thy peace:
For I am with thee, and no man shall set on thee to hurt thee: for I have much people in this city.
And he continued there a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them.

12.pericope_label: And when Gallio was the deputy of Achaia, the Jews made insurrection with one accord against Paul, and brought him to the judgment seat

schools.summary: Robertson alone can date the scene, from a Delphi inscription naming Gallio proconsul and fixing Paul at Corinth in A.D. 50-52, and he makes the point a manifesto: "it is amazing how Luke is confirmed whenever a new discovery is made." Ellicott credits Luke's accuracy in official titles, though the two differ quietly on when Achaia passed back to the senate. Both correct the English — Ellicott objecting to "insurrection", Robertson finding a double compound meaning a rush at Paul — and Ellicott is certain the charge invoked Roman rather than Mosaic law, while Robertson concedes a double meaning but denies Jewish law any standing before a proconsul.

Calvin offers two motives for the sudden move after a year of quiet: a new deputy emboldened them, "as froward men use to abuse new things", or they expected his favour. He reads the charge as innovation against the law of God, calling the Roman construction "cold" and "forced", and then turns the episode into a doctrine of the magistrate: Rome left provincial religion alone only because it had no truth of its own, whereas "nothing is more absurd than to leave the worship of God to men's choice". Gill supplies the geography of Achaia and Gallio's flight from a fever by ship.

Clarke gathers the classical testimonia to Gallio's sweetness of temper and supplies his end under Nero, and notes that the Jews had to come to the governor because they had no power to punish in a Roman province — "had the Jews possessed the power here, Paul had been put to death!" Wesley admires the man's generosity of temper and then withholds the last word: "Yet one thing he lacked! But he knew it not and had no concern about it."

Henry attacks the accusation by way of the toleration that made it possible: the Romans allowed the Jews their own law, but does a permission to keep it include a right to impose it? "Must those therefore be prosecuted as criminals who worship God in any other way?" He adds that their own law promised a prophet whom they should hear, so that Paul's preaching was perfective of it rather than contrary to it.

debates.question: Which law did the Jews accuse Paul of contravening?

positions.view: Rome's — Judaism was a licensed religion and the charge was that Paul preached a new one that was not.
God's — the Roman reading is "cold" and "forced"; they charged him with altering the worship prescribed in the law so as to convict him of innovation.
Both at once — Clarke putting the argument in the accusers' mouths: he is not a Jew, for he does not admit circumcision; not a Gentile, for he preaches against the gods.
The phrase has a double meaning, but Jewish law had no standing before Gallio, and no evidence for a breach of Roman law was produced.

debates.question: When did Achaia pass from the emperor back to the senate?

positions.view: In the same year as the expulsion of the Jews from Rome.
In A.D. 44, when Claudius restored it with proconsul as the governor's title.

outliers.view: Alone has access to the Delphi inscription — a letter of Claudius naming Gallio proconsul of Achaia — which fixes the date of Paul's Corinthian ministry and which none of the older commentators could use.

themes: And when Gallio was the deputy of Achaia, the Jews made insurrection with one accord against Paul, and brought him to the judgment seat,
Saying, This fellow persuadeth men to worship God contrary to the law.

14.pericope_label: And when Paul was now about to open his mouth, Gallio said unto the Jews, If it were a matter of wrong or wicked lewdness

schools.summary: The grammarians show that Gallio's apparent concession is hollow: Robertson identifies the condition as one determined as unfulfilled, so "the Jews had no case against Paul in a Roman court", while Ellicott hears the same as tone — "the very turn of the phrase expresses an intense impatience". They translate the two crime-words four ways between them, Barnes making the second the deed of a veteran offender and Robertson a "slick citizen". Ellicott catches the pronoun in "your law" and draws the comparison with Pilate; Robertson alone traces what the ruling did, leaving the movement a form of Judaism and so opening the empire to Paul's preaching.

Calvin refuses to congratulate Gallio. He concedes the nation was contentious and that Paul himself rebukes trifling over words, but "Gallio is not worthy to be excused who doth mock the holy law of God together with their curiosity", since "when the worship of God is in hand, the strife is not about words, but a matter of all other most serious is handled". Gill notes that the Jews were dismissed with a warning not to return.

Clarke makes the ruling a landmark of liberty: "a better answer could not be given by man", the state having no right to control any man's religious opinion, and had every ruler acted so the persecution laws that remain "blots and disgraces on the statute books of almost all the civilized nations of Europe" would be unwritten. Wesley reads the manner rather than the doctrine — "he speaks with the utmost coolness and contempt" — then turns it on the reader, since the question of the name of Jesus "is of more importance than all things else under heaven".

debates.question: What is the moral value of Gallio's refusal to judge?

positions.view: It is exemplary — "a better answer could not be given by man"; the magistrate has no business restraining the free teaching of conscience where the state is not endangered.
It is contemptuous — he mocks the law of God along with their curiosity, treating as mere words a matter of the utmost seriousness.
Neither praise nor blame of the ruling, but of the manner: he speaks "with the utmost coolness and contempt" about a question of more importance than anything under heaven.

debates.question: Was anyone struck when the court was cleared?

positions.view: No — the verb denotes no violence, only an authoritative dismission, Gill adding that they left under warning.
Yes — the lictors were ordered to clear the court, and those who did not retreat at once "were exposed to the ignominy of blows from their rods".

outliers.view: Alone reads the decision constitutionally rather than morally: it established nothing in favour of Christianity, only left it a form of Judaism and so not against Roman law — which "opened the door for Paul's preaching all over the Roman Empire".

themes: And when Paul was now about to open his mouth, Gallio said unto the Jews, If it were a matter of wrong or wicked lewdness, O ye Jews, reason would that I should bear with you:
But if it be a question of words and names, and of your law, look ye to it; for I will be no judge of such matters.
And he drave them from the judgment seat.

17.pericope_label: Then all the Greeks took Sosthenes, the chief ruler of the synagogue, and beat him before the judgment seat. And Gallio cared for none of those things

schools.summary: Barnes takes the Greek bystanders literally and reads pagan indignation at Jewish bigotry; Ellicott and Robertson take "Greeks" for an interpolation and make the assault an attack by the Jews on their own failed leader. All three defend Gallio against the proverb built on him — Barnes denying any propriety in preaching the verse against worldly men, Robertson calling the charge "quite beside the mark" and praising "a clear headed judge who would not be led astray by Jewish subterfuges". Ellicott alone then supplies the sequel that undercuts the defence: the same easy temper served Nero's vices.

Calvin prosecutes where the others acquit. Gallio's indifference was contempt for the religion rather than sluggishness — Rome licensed vows to every idol, yet "in the common liberty of all manner of superstition, only true religion was excepted" — so he winked at the beating, wanting the Jews to destroy each other. And the verdict is not Calvin's own: "by the mouth of Luke, the Spirit condemneth Gallio's carelessness, because he did not aid a man who was unjustly punished." Gill takes the assailants to be profane Greeks emboldened by the dismissal.

Clarke assembles the manuscript case against the word "Greeks" and argues that Jews beating one of their own rulers "through envy at his conversion" is far more likely; he doubts Gallio even saw the assault, defends him against censure as "manifest injustice", and takes the resort to blows as proof of a bad cause — "manual logic". Wesley reads Sosthenes as probably Paul's chief accuser, beaten by his own party for wasting their time, and cannot believe it happened in Gallio's sight.

debates.question: Who beat Sosthenes?

positions.view: Greeks — pagan bystanders indignant at the Jews' bigotry and encouraged by Gallio's dismissal, though Barnes notes some copies read "Jews".
Jews — "Greeks" is absent from the best manuscripts and the fathers, and it is far likelier that they turned on their own ruler, whether for treachery or for failure.

debates.question: Which side was Sosthenes on?

positions.view: Already leaning to Paul — Calvin calling him one of Paul's companions and advocates — so the blows punish defection.
Paul's chief accuser, beaten by his own party for having wasted their time to no purpose.
Not yet converted; the conversion came later, Robertson noting drily that "the beating did Sosthenes good".

debates.question: Did Sosthenes deserve the beating?

positions.view: He "richly deserved" it; the affair was a police-court matter beneath a proconsul's notice.
He was guiltless and unjustly punished, and the failure to protect him is what the passage condemns.

debates.question: Did Gallio witness the assault?

positions.view: Yes — it happened before the tribunal, and the Jews did not shrink from venting their rage in his presence.
Probably not — it happened as the court broke up or after he had left, Wesley thinking it can hardly have been in his sight.

outliers.view: Alone follows Gallio out of the chapter and lets the biography qualify the exegesis: the easy gentleness that reads so well here left him unfit to resist Nero's court, where he shared in ministering to the emperor's vices before ending under his displeasure.

themes: Then all the Greeks took Sosthenes, the chief ruler of the synagogue, and beat him before the judgment seat. And Gallio cared for none of those things.

18.pericope_label: And Paul after this tarried there yet a good while, and then took his leave of the brethren, and sailed thence into Syria... having shorn his head in Cenchrea: for he had a vow

schools.summary: Ellicott is confident the vow was the temporary Nazarite of Numbers 6 and solves the awkwardness of cropping rather than growing the hair by the difference between being shorn and being shaved, with the clippings still owed to the Temple — which explains the haste to reach the feast. He argues for Paul rather than Aquila on two grounds, and offers thankfulness after fear and the all-things-to-all-men principle as motives. Robertson denies the Nazarite identification outright, since such a vow could be absolved only at Jerusalem, and ends in candour about what kind of vow it was; Barnes describes the institution at length and then withdraws — "where nothing is recorded, conjecture is useless".

Calvin makes the reversal at Corinth significant: elsewhere Paul fled at once because his presence drew rage on the whole church, but with their malice bridled "he had rather sting and nettle them, than by departing minister unto them any new occasion of rage". On the vow he denies Paul acted for his own sake at all — it would be absurd "for him to bind his own conscience with that religion from which he had loosed all other men" — reading it wholly as accommodation, and then turns it against Rome's use of the passage to authorise vows.

Clarke supplies the legal reason for the safety, that after Gallio's ruling no state persecution was possible and citizenship made Paul's person "sacred", and then sets out the whole roll-call of authorities on both sides of the Paul-or-Aquila question before concluding that "the bare letter of the text determines nothing" and leaning to Paul. He records the versions that solved it by making the verb plural. Wesley simply prints the shaving as Aquila's act.

Henry sees no harm in referring the vow to either man, noting only that some throw it on Aquila as a Jew who "retained perhaps more of his Judaism than was convenient", and defends the Nazarite institution as having "a great deal of moral and very pious significance", fit to die last of all the Jewish ceremonies.

Chrysostom reads the whole scene as the old order dissolving — "see how the Law was breaking up; see how they were bound by conscience" — and notices the defect nobody else does: shearing the head with a vow was the Jewish custom, "but then there ought to be also a sacrifice, which was not the case here".

debates.question: Who was shorn at Cenchrea — Paul or Aquila?

positions.view: Paul, with "hardly the shadow of a doubt": a vow would have obliged Aquila to go to Jerusalem instead of staying at Ephesus, and the neighbouring participles are Paul's.
Aquila — printed as his act without argument.

The text does not settle it; Clarke lists the fathers and moderns on both sides before leaning to Paul, Calvin says "neither skilleth it much", Henry sees no harm either way, and Barnes says only that the connection requires Paul.

debates.question: Was it a Nazarite vow?

positions.view: Yes — the temporary Nazarite of Numbers 6, completed later at the Temple by one who was outside Palestine when the term expired.
No — such a vow "could be absolved only in Jerusalem"; the hair was probably only trimmed, and what kind of vow it was is simply not clear.
The custom was Jewish, but the required sacrifice is missing, so the rite as performed is defective.

outliers.view: Alone turns the vow into controversy with Rome: since "Paul was moved with no religion to make his vow", the passage cannot authorise vow-making, and there is all the difference between tolerating an old rite until it dies out and reviving a dead one.

themes: And Paul after this tarried there yet a good while, and then took his leave of the brethren, and sailed thence into Syria, and with him Priscilla and Aquila; having shorn his head in Cenchrea: for he had a vow.

19.pericope_label: And he came to Ephesus, and left them there... I must by all means keep this feast that cometh in Jerusalem

schools.summary: Barnes and Ellicott set out what Ephesus was — the Artemis temple, the meeting of East and West that made Greek religion "fruitful in magic, and mysteries, and charms" — and Barnes quotes Chandler on its ruin. Ellicott notes the better reading "they came", doubts the clause about the feast is even Luke's, argues for Pentecost against the passover, and thinks the bare verse hides a great deal: a possible shipwreck, Philip at Caesarea, the vow completed, and the clash with Peter of Galatians 2. Robertson builds the case that the unnamed city is Jerusalem from idiom, direction and the absence of any errand at Caesarea, and places the Galatians incident earlier than Ellicott does.

Calvin finds the refusal to stay at Ephesus genuinely strange, since Paul was heard more patiently there than anywhere and was asked to remain, and infers "that he had some great cause to go up to Jerusalem in haste". Of the return journey he insists it was not idle: strengthening all the disciples cost "great pains-taking", since he was enforced to go hither and thither and often turn out of his way. Gill supplies the antiquarian history of the city's many names.

Clarke reads on past Chandler's account into the goats, crows and partridge of the ruined stadium and theatre, and ends on the seven churches — "the Church of Ephesus is blotted out of the map of Christianity! Be silent and adore." He reports that the whole clause about keeping the feast is missing from the oldest manuscripts and four versions, with Griesbach flagging it doubtful, yet takes the feast to be the passover; and he identifies the church saluted as Jerusalem, "the Mother, or Apostolic Church", from which even Rome was only a daughter. Wesley denies Paul went from any conscience of obligation to Jewish feasts.

Chrysostom gives the reason for leaving the couple behind that nobody else states plainly — Paul left them at Ephesus "that they should teach" — and pauses over the order of the names to remark, "lo, a woman also".

debates.question: Which feast was Paul hurrying to keep?

positions.view: The passover, at which he could meet the greatest number of his countrymen.
Pentecost — miss it and nothing falls before Tabernacles, by which season sailing is dangerous.

debates.question: Is the clause about keeping the feast genuine?

positions.view: Doubtful — it is missing from the oldest manuscripts and several versions; Griesbach flagged it and White thought it probably to be struck out, Robertson guessing it was added to explain the "going up" of the next verse.
Treat it as text and expound it, differing only over which feast and why he went.

debates.question: Where does the confrontation with Peter of Galatians 2:11 belong?

positions.view: At this visit to Antioch, the Judaising party having gathered strength during Paul's long absence.
Earlier — at Paul's previous stay in Antioch, not this one.

outliers.view: Supplies the purpose of leaving Priscilla and Aquila at Ephesus — "with good reason, namely, that they should teach" — and stops to notice the woman named first, adding that Paul did not yet withdraw the couple from their Jewish customs.

themes: And he came to Ephesus, and left them there: but he himself entered into the synagogue, and reasoned with the Jews.
When they desired him to tarry longer time with them, he consented not;
But bade them farewell, saying, I must by all means keep this feast that cometh in Jerusalem: but I will return again unto you, if God will. And he sailed from Ephesus.
And when he had landed at Cesarea, and gone up, and saluted the church, he went down to Antioch.
And after he had spent some time there, he departed, and went over all the country of Galatia and Phrygia in order, strengthening all the disciples.

24.pericope_label: And a certain Jew named Apollos, born at Alexandria, an eloquent man, and mighty in the scriptures, came to Ephesus

schools.summary: Robertson sets Apollos in an Alexandria where Jews were a third of the population and Jewish-Alexandrian philosophy was growing under a Philo still living, defuses the name as a contraction of Apollonius, and turns "mighty in the Scriptures" into a charge against the ministry — "there is no excuse for ignorance of the Scriptures on the part of preachers". Ellicott goes much further, arguing from Luther's guess about Hebrews and from parallels with the Wisdom of Solomon that Apollos wrote both, and traces to him the entry of the Philonic Logos into Christian thought; he also notes that the adjective rendered "eloquent" implies learning as much as speech.

Calvin reads the timing as providence — Paul is driven from Ephesus and "Apollos cometh in his place to supply his absence" — and then weighs whether eloquence befits a minister at all. Paul was denied it so that "the power of the Spirit might appear more excellent in his rude and homely speech", yet that lack "did no whit let but that the Lord might choose to himself eloquent ministers". On being mighty in the Scriptures he withholds the credit from the man: the force belongs to Scripture, "that it hath sufficient force both to defend the truth, and also to refute the subtilty of Satan".

Clarke finds it strange that a Jew should bear a false god's name and conjectures Gentile parents who came over to Judaism after their son was named; he then wanders through Alexandria from the Pharos to Bonaparte's capture of the city. Wesley states the governing rule in a line: "every talent may be of use in the kingdom of God, if joined with the knowledge of the Scriptures and fervour of spirit."

Henry explains why the narrative leaves Paul travelling to introduce Apollos — without this paragraph parts of Paul's letters cannot be understood — insists the name "was not Apollo, the name of one of the heathen gods", collects the renderings of the word for eloquent, and draws the distinction that matters: many could quote texts off-hand and had only "the form of knowledge, and the letter of the law", whereas Apollos understood their sense, so that "a convincing, commanding, confirming power went along with all his expositions".

debates.question: Is Apollos named after the heathen god?

positions.view: No — the name "was not Apollo, the name of one of the heathen gods, but Apollos", and may be the Apelles of Romans 16:10.
Yes — "for so we should write the word"; it is strange in a Jew, and suggests Gentile parents who converted after naming him.
The question does not arise: it is a contraction of Apollonius or Apollodorus, and Codex Bezae has the longer form.

debates.question: Does the word rendered "eloquent" mean speech or learning?

positions.view: Either — a man of words or a man of ideas, since the root covers both; Apollos was doubtless both.
It "implies learning as well as eloquence", and was used above all of historians.
Collects the renderings without choosing: a prudent man, a learned man, a good historian, one who could speak well, "an oracle of a man".

outliers.view: Advances the boldest claim in the chapter, arguing that the close agreement of style and language between the Wisdom of Solomon and the Epistle to the Hebrews makes it "scarcely possible to resist the inference that they must have come from the same pen", representing "different stages in the spiritual growth of the same man" — Apollos.

themes: And a certain Jew named Apollos, born at Alexandria, an eloquent man, and mighty in the scriptures, came to Ephesus.

25.pericope_label: This man was instructed in the way of the Lord; and being fervent in the spirit... knowing only the baptism of John

schools.summary: Ellicott identifies the verb that later gave the Church its catechumens, concludes the Baptist's influence reached as far as Alexandria, and reconstructs precisely what Apollos lacked — a teacher who never passed the Baptist's standpoint, so that "the Christ was for him the head of a glorified Judaism". Barnes contradicts him flatly, holding that Apollos had not yet heard Jesus was the Messiah at all; Robertson takes the middle line and adds the root sense of teaching by dinning into the ears. On the fervent spirit Ellicott insists the noun means the man's own; on rebaptism Robertson denies what Ellicott thinks nearly necessary.

Calvin makes the pairing of zeal and knowledge the lesson: "doctrine without zeal is either like a sword in the hand of a madman, or else it lieth still as cold and without use", yet knowledge must come first and govern it. He reads "the baptism of John" as covering the Baptist's whole ministry and draws from it a rule that it is "wickedness and impious profanation" to separate sacraments from doctrine. On Priscilla he praises, then restricts: she taught "at home in her own house, that she might not overthrow the order prescribed by God and nature". Gill guesses the teachers were parents once John's disciples.

Clarke defends the text against a proposed negative — "surely it is possible for a man to teach accurately what he knows" — and presses the scene on his male readers: a public teacher, eloquent and mighty in the Scriptures, "was not ashamed to be indebted to the instructions of a Christian woman".

Chrysostom raised the difficulty first and could not settle it: if Apollos knew only John's baptism, how was he fervent in the Spirit, and did the expounding "more perfectly" mean he needed to be baptised? The text records none, "and it is likely that he did in fact receive baptism".

debates.question: What did Apollos not yet know?

positions.view: He knew the life, death and resurrection and accepted Jesus as Christ, but from a teacher who never passed the Baptist's standpoint, so he had not learnt that circumcision was nothing or that the Temple ordinances were passing away.
"It is clear that he had not heard that Jesus was the Messiah"; he had only the right expectation of a humble and suffering deliverer, drawn from the Old Testament.
He knew what the Baptist knew at his death — including that Jesus was the Son of God — but not the Cross, the Resurrection or Pentecost.

debates.question: Whose spirit was fervent?

positions.view: The man's own — the noun is used as in Romans 12:11, "not for the Holy Spirit of God".
The Holy Spirit's — Luke "doth attribute zeal to the Spirit", and Apollos was moved not by the instinct of his own mind but by the Spirit's motion.

debates.question: Was Apollos baptised again after being taught?

positions.view: It follows "almost necessarily", by the parallel of the disciples in the next chapter, that he was baptised into the name of the Lord Jesus.
"He was not rebaptized, but only received fuller information."
Cannot decide — no baptism is recorded, "and it is likely that he did in fact receive baptism".

outliers.view: Uses Priscilla's teaching against Rome — women were not then so ignorant of the word as the Papists would have them, since "one of the chief teachers of the Church was instructed by a woman" — and in the same breath confines the precedent to the house, "that she might not overthrow the order prescribed by God and nature".

themes: This man was instructed in the way of the Lord; and being fervent in the spirit, he spake and taught diligently the things of the Lord, knowing only the baptism of John.
And he began to speak boldly in the synagogue: whom when Aquila and Priscilla had heard, they took him unto them, and expounded unto him the way of God more perfectly.

27.pericope_label: And when he was disposed to pass into Achaia, the brethren wrote, exhorting the disciples to receive him

schools.summary: Ellicott identifies the letter as "the first instance of what were afterwards known technically as letters of commendation" and reconstructs its afterlife: the Corinthian partisans held it up as a point in which Apollos excelled Paul, who answered that the church he planted was itself an epistle known and read of all men. Robertson traces the same line to the same verse. Ellicott also grants Apollos a larger success with Jews than Paul had, by a Philonic route, while Robertson takes the imperfect of the rare double compound to mean only that "he had the last word". Barnes uses the resulting factions to praise Paul's freedom from envy.

Calvin reads the commendation as more than hospitality: the Corinthians were asked not merely to lodge the man but "that they should suffer him to teach", lest the gifts given for edifying "lie buried". From the encounter he builds a doctrine of Scripture — if the law and the prophets sufficed for Apollos to prove Jesus is the Christ "as if he did point out the matter with his finger", it is "detestable blasphemy" to call Scripture dark, and refusing to dispute out of Scripture stands refuted by Luke. Gill has the Jews "refuted over and over, and confounded to the last degree".

Clarke translates the long Codex Bezae addition, in which visiting Corinthians beg Apollos to cross over with them, and reports that "through grace" is absent from several copies. He calls Apollos "the innocent cause of a sort of schism" at Corinth and records Jerome's claim that he became bishop there. Wesley states the principle behind the disputed phrase — "it is through grace only that any gift of any one is profitable to another" — and judges that Apollos "was better able to convince the Jews, than to convert the heathens".

debates.question: Did Apollos actually convince the Jews?

positions.view: Yes — they were confounded to the last degree, all opposition borne down and effectually silenced.
No — the verb stands in the imperfect, which "does not mean that Apollos convinced these rabbis, but he had the last word".

debates.question: Does "through grace" belong with helping or with believing?

positions.view: With helping — grace working alongside the gift of wisdom enabled Apollos to raise men to a higher stage of thought.
Either is possible; the translators took the obvious course and tied it to believing.
Declines to choose — "both are true as the references show".

outliers.view: Alone allows that Apollos outdid Paul on his own ground: arguing after the manner of Hebrews rather than Galatians, and treating hearers as men pressing on to maturity rather than children fed with milk, gave him "a larger measure of real or apparent success in dealing with the Jews than had attended the labours of St. Paul".

themes: And when he was disposed to pass into Achaia, the brethren wrote, exhorting the disciples to receive him: who, when he was come, helped them much which had believed through grace:
For he mightily convinced the Jews, and that publickly, shewing by the scriptures that Jesus was Christ.
